title: The Slow Glasshouse
premise: Ulyana Halloran, a bridge inspector who measures everything—including her own marriage—in millimeters of wear, discovers a box of undelivered letters behind her late mother's wardrobe, addressed to a man in the old neighborhood slated for demolition. As she traces the letters' intended recipient, she uncovers the love affair her mother abandoned for duty, and recognizes her own marriage corroding along the same joints. When the last bus route to the old neighborhood is permanently rerouted, Ulyana must deliver the letters herself and speak her mother's goodbye aloud—then choose whether her own life will be another bridge maintained out of obligation or one she crosses on purpose. She delivers the letters, says goodbye properly at last, and walks home to tell her husband the truth: that she is staying, but not out of duty.
about_author: J. M. Zhou is the pen name of a former civil engineer who spent eleven years inspecting bridges across the American Midwest before turning to fiction. Their stories about infrastructure and intimacy have appeared in several small literary journals.

chapters.title: Expansion Joints
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. On a routine inspection of the Halsted viaduct, Ulyana measures hairline fractures with the same detached precision she applies to her marriage to Tom, a man she loves like maintenance. At home, clearing her dead mother's flat, she finds a box behind the wardrobe: forty letters, sealed, never sent. Emotional beat: the first crack of curiosity breaking through numbness.

chapters.title: The Undelivered
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. She reads the first letter against every instinct toward privacy and learns her mother loved a man named Emil Kowalczyk, a glassblower from the old neighborhood, and chose duty—a sick husband, a child—over him. The letters stop mid-correspondence in 1987. Emotional beat: grief complicated by anger at a mother she thought she knew.

chapters.title: Route 61
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. She learns the old neighborhood is being demolished and the 61 bus—the only line that still serves it—is being rerouted in six weeks. Her city councilman cousin, Denny, dismisses her questions about preservation; power, she notes, smooths over what it displaces. Emotional beat: urgency hardening into resolve.

chapters.title: The Glasshouse
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. She finds Emil, ninety-one, living in a sagging Victorian greenhouse-turned-workshop, still making slow glass—panes said to show events years delayed. He knows exactly who she is the moment he sees her face. He refuses the letters unopened. Emotional beat: awe shadowed by rejection; the past is not sentimental.

chapters.title: What Tom Doesn't Say
chapters.summary: Tom's POV. Tom notices his wife disappearing into someone else's history and confronts his own complicity: he proposed because it was sensible, and she accepted because it was expected. He finds her asleep over the letters and, instead of waking her, reads one. Emotional beat: his quiet devastation—and the first honest thing he has felt in years.

chapters.title: Slow Glass
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. Emil finally lets her in, showing her a pane he made the year her mother left: through it, the street outside appears as it was decades ago. He explains why he never answered—her mother's final letter asked him to let her go, and obeying was his penance. Emotional beat: understanding without absolution.

chapters.title: Denny's Offer
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. Denny offers Ulyana a promotion—chief inspector, her dream—if she stops asking about the neighborhood and signs off on the demolition survey early. The corruption is polite, reasonable, almost kind. That night she lies awake measuring what her integrity weighs. Emotional beat: temptation as a mirror; power corrupts by offering comfort.

chapters.title: Fracture
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Ulyana refuses Denny and loses the promotion; Tom, having read everything, asks her directly whether their marriage is duty or choice—and she cannot answer. They fight with the precision of people who know each other's load limits. Emotional beat: climax of the marriage arc; everything hidden is finally spoken, badly.

chapters.title: The Last Bus
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. On the final day of Route 61, Ulyana brings Emil aboard with the box of letters. Riding the old route past vanished storefronts, she reads her mother's goodbye aloud while Emil watches the street through a pane of his own slow glass, seeing her mother young on the corner where she once waited. Emotional beat: catharsis; the goodbye finally delivered, out loud, before the route dies.

chapters.title: Load Rating
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV, coda. Months later, Ulyana inspects a new pedestrian bridge built where the neighborhood stood, and files an honest report that delays its opening—small defiance, real cost. At home, she and Tom begin again without pretense, choosing each other daily rather than once. Emotional beat: quiet resolution; love rebuilt not as maintenance but as deliberate crossing.
